a16z's Martin Casado on why the word "pacing" was a misstep, and Databricks' @alighodsi on what the labs were actually asking for:

Martin: "Saying security and safety is important, it is with every tech epoch, and we wanna have some oversight. That was very, very sensible. The problem was just couching this notion of pacing."

"There's a number of issues with pacing. First off, it's orthogonal to safety and security. You can slowly build a weapon. That's not different than building a weapon."

"It kind of feels like this kind of almost milquetoast capitulation to the pause people. 'You say pause, well, I say pacing.' Which is almost like pause, but it's not like pause."

Ali: "They're saying, 'Hey, if we do that, it'll slow us down. And I'm not sure the other side is doing that. So can you guys come in and slow us down? Put some guardrails around us. We'll happily then follow the rules and do the secure thing. Otherwise it doesn't make sense 'cause we'll get our butts kicked.'"

Martin: "Nuanced second-order words don't work when people are really afraid... I literally think you should have just been like, 'Safety and security is paramount. We're gonna put in these controls.'"

"Dario's first five words or whatever are, 'We need to pace the frontier.' It just puts you in a very different mindset. What he could have said is, 'We need to secure the frontier.'"

"Pace is like the uncanny valley of making the doomer people unhappy and the policy people unhappy. The doomer people are like, 'That's not a pause, this is pacing.' And everybody else is like, 'This isn't real, you're not gonna do it anyways, and you're not as focused on security.'"

@alighodsi @martin_casado @sarahdingwang

Databricks' @alighodsi says "Right now the existential risk is close to zero." Why he thinks the public doom talk is irresponsible:

"Leaders have responsibility to not freak people out unnecessarily unless there's really, really good reason."

"Talking about these kind of existential risks and scenarios where all of humanity's gonna be wiped out, I think is irresponsible. It can tip a lot of people over, and it can cause a lot of mental health issues."

"If there is an actual reason for it, that's a different story. But I think that right now the existential risk is close to zero. So why freak everybody out? It's not actually needed. There are risks. We'll get into it. That's probably where we disagree."

"First and foremost, I think leaders should not freak everyone out."

"If there's technical nuances in how we're doing AI research, researchers can discuss that. You don't need to every time go on TV and blast on Twitter to millions of people that 'I think there's like this 10% risk that all humanity is gonna be wiped out.'"

"I think it causes a lot of harm for a lot of folks who get stressed out and actually are not in the nuances of all of this stuff and what it means."

@alighodsi @sarahdingwang @martin_casado

tweets.text:
With oil and tech stocks surging, the consumer sector has become increasingly irrelevant:

Consumer Discretionary and Consumer Staples sectors now account for ~13% of the S&P 500’s market cap, their lowest proportion since at least the 1990s.

This figure has declined another -5 percentage points since 2022.

By comparison, this weight averaged ~22% over the last 35 years and bottomed at ~16% during the 2000 Dot-Com Bubble.

This comes as Consumer Discretionary now represents ~9% of the S&P 500’s market cap, its lowest proportion since the 2008 Financial Crisis.

At the same time, Consumer Staples accounts for just ~4%, its lowest since at least the 1990s.

Consumer stocks have been left in the dust.

tweets.text:
Databricks' @alighodsi with a16z's Martin Casado on who should be policing the AI labs:

Martin: "There's kind of three proposals. The OpenAI, Anthropic one is a third party. The Elon Musk one, as far as I can tell, is the labs cross-check each other like peer review, like you do in science. And then the Mark Zuckerberg one is police yourself."

Ali: "If we have boxing matches in the ring, the boxers should just be the judges of each other. Would that work? No. They would scream foul all the time."

"When vested interests are at play and there's like IPO plans and these two companies are so competitive and they have this history also between them, yeah, they'll be *very* fair to each other."

"That's why you need a third party. Why do we have judges in the world at all? Why do we have third parties at all? Why can't people just figure things out between themselves?"

"They should try. If they want to do it, they should try. But I'm skeptical that they wouldn't just be biased in multiple ways to judge each other."

@alighodsi @martin_casado @sarahdingwang

The biggest foreign buyer of US assets just got a reason to go home.

The Bank of Japan hiked to 1.25%, its highest since 1995. Japanese investors hold about $2.5 trillion in US stocks and bonds, plus $1.1 trillion in Treasurys, more than any other country.

For 30 years, near-zero rates at home sent that cash into US markets. Now home pays too. If even part of that money turns around, it pulls a steady bid out of US stocks and pushes Treasury yields higher.

Since 1985, most of the rise in the top 1% income share, 5.8 of 10.5 points, came from pass-through businesses. Car dealers, law firms, medical practices, contractors. About 3 million owners, worth roughly 10x the Forbes 400 combined.

The path to wealth is boring: own a profitable business, not chase the next hot stock.

A lot of the insufferable $GLXY maxis on this app don’t seem to realize what they’re actually buying:

​Galaxy uses an Up-C structure. Public shareholders own Class A stock in a topco, while Novogratz and insiders hold the real asset down in the operating partnership.

​This creates issues including -->

​>a Tax Receivable Agreement (TRA) where 85% of the cash tax benefits go to legacy partners instead of the pubco balance sheet
>​Class B voting shares and a side director nomination deal that cements insider board control.

​It’s completely legal, but let’s not pretend public common shares are treated as first-class citizens here.

And for a Democrat like Novogratz, hardly a "power to the people" structute. 

I'd happily change my mind if these facts do.

One question that rarely gets asked is where future AI computation will take place. 

Back in the 1960s, the prevailing wisdom was that computation would be performed by huge, room-sized computers. However, rather than ever-bigger mainframes, we got personal computers.

My guess is that something similar will happen to AI. The quality of local models is rapidly approaching that of frontier models. Once AI becomes embodied in the physical world, be it through humanoid robots or self-driving vehicles, local model access will be preferable to a remote connection to a distant data center.

tweets.text: Stephen Wolfram has coined the phrase “computational irreducibility.” Wolfram’s point is that there are no shortcuts in predicting what a sufficiently complex system will do. If you want to know what a system will do ten steps ahead, in most cases, the best that you can do is run through all ten steps. This is a huge problem for AI safety because it implies that one might not be able to predict, even in principle, what an AI system will do until it has done it. I assume Anthropic knows this?

Analysts expect the hyperscalers to incur $255 billion in depreciation charges in 2026 on capex of $784 billion. The depreciation charge is projected to rise to $581 billion in 2029 on capex of $1.16 trillion. 

To put things in context, the hyperscalers are expected to generate $569 billion in operating profits in 2026. 

I should also add that these numbers exclude off-balance sheet capex, which is likely to add another $200 billion to hyperscaler spending. This means that annual hyperscaler capex, if analyst estimates are to be believed, will be around $1.4 trillion by the end of the decade.
